pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–13 years

- **Topic:** Pure Substances & Mixtures

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry 'Pure and impure substances'):** The concept of a pure substance; mixtures, including dissolving; the identification of pure substances. (The 'formulation' idea — a useful mixture made to a precise composition — is GCSE/KS4 content.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-2 supporting):** Each pure substance has characteristic properties (e.g. a fixed melting/boiling point) used to identify it and distinguish it from a mixture.

- **Operational details:** The scientific meaning of PURE differs sharply from everyday use ('pure orange juice' is actually a mixture): in chemistry a pure substance is a single element or compound with nothing else in it, while a mixture contains two or more substances not chemically joined. The powerful, testable idea is that a pure substance has a SHARP, FIXED melting and boiling point, whereas a mixture melts/boils over a RANGE of temperatures and at shifted values (e.g. salty water boils above 100°C and freezes below 0°C). So melting/boiling behaviour is a PURITY TEST. Teach by comparing heating curves of a pure sample (flat plateau at one temperature) versus an impure one (sloped/spread transition). Formulations (deliberately designed useful mixtures like paint, medicines, alloys) can be previewed as a bridge to KS4. Reinforce that a mixture keeps its components' properties and can be separated physically.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal). The child distinguishes the chemical meaning of 'pure' from everyday usage, and uses a melting/boiling point (sharp vs range) to judge whether a sample is pure or a mixture.
bestPractices: Separate the chemistry meaning of 'pure' (single substance) from the everyday meaning (natural/unadulterated).
Make melting/boiling behaviour a PURITY TEST: sharp fixed point = pure, range = mixture.
Compare pure and impure heating curves side by side so the difference is observed.
Reinforce that a mixture keeps its components' properties and separates physically.
Preview formulations (paint, medicines, alloys) as designed useful mixtures, flagged as KS4.
keyRepresentations: Side-by-side heating curves: sharp plateau (pure) vs sloped range (mixture)
A salt-in-water demo shifting boiling above 100°C / freezing below 0°C
commonMisconceptions: 'Pure' means natural/healthy/unprocessed rather than a single substance.
A mixture and a compound are the same because both contain more than one element.
Adding salt to water raises its freezing point / doesn't change its boiling point.
Pure and impure samples melt at the same temperature.

learn.summary: Learners aged 11–13 distinguish the chemical meaning of 'pure' (a single element or compound with nothing else in it) from the everyday advertising sense ('natural/unadulterated'), and use melting/boiling behaviour as a purity test: at a given pressure a pure substance melts/boils at one sharp fixed temperature, while a mixture typically melts/boils over a range and at shifted values. The core activity is an empirical heating-curve comparison where learners observe the contrast rather than being told the rule; supporting activities add particle-level contrast, meaning-of-'pure' reference work, and categorisation/graph-reading practice. Formulations (deliberately designed useful mixtures such as paint, medicines, alloys) are previewed as a bridge to later (KS4) study.

activities.title: Purity tester: reading heating curves of pure vs impure samples
feedback: If a learner expects both samples to hold at exactly 0°C, point to the salty-ice curve: it starts melting below 0°C and melts over a spread rather than at one clean plateau — this is the typical signature of a mixture. Salt is spread on icy roads because dissolved salt lowers the temperature at which ice melts.
If a learner judges a mystery sample by its final temperature only, redirect attention to the shape: a sharp flat step means pure, a sloped spread means a mixture.

If a learner says a solid that melts over 78–85°C is pure, note that a wide range (rather than a single sharp value) signals a mixture; a pure sample of the substance would melt sharply at one fixed temperature, usually a little higher than where the impure sample started melting.
activities.rationale: Purity becomes concrete when learners test it and observe the contrast, so 'melting point is a purity test' is an observed result rather than a stated rule. Comparing pure and impure heating curves side by side makes the sharp-plateau vs sloped-range difference visible, and matches the standards' emphasis on characteristic fixed melting/boiling points used to identify substances.
sourceClaims: A pure substance has a sharp fixed melting/boiling point; a mixture melts/boils over a range — used as a purity test; characteristic properties identify substances (NGSS PS1.A)
learnerActions: Heat a sample of ice made from distilled water, stirring it, and watch a temperature-vs-time graph: observe that it stays roughly flat at about 0°C (at normal air pressure) while it melts, then climbs once it has fully melted.

Beside it, heat frozen salt water and observe that it starts melting below 0°C and that its temperature creeps up while it melts, instead of holding at one clean plateau. The exact temperatures depend on how salty the water is.

State in your own words what the SHAPE of each curve shows: one sharp flat step suggests a pure substance; a sloped spread across a range suggests a mixture (a useful rule at this level, although a few special mixtures can also change state sharply).
Take a 'mystery sample' round: given unknown heating curves, judge whether each sample is pure or a mixture and give your reason from the curve shape.

As a bonus, heat salty water next to pure water under the same conditions and compare. The salty water starts boiling at a slightly higher temperature (usually only about a degree, even with a lot of salt), and its temperature keeps creeping up as water boils away and the solution gets saltier. This shows that impurities both shift AND spread the transition.
activities.intendedInsight: A thermometer can act as a purity detector: at a given pressure a pure substance changes state at a single sharp fixed temperature, while a mixture usually changes state over a range and at shifted values — so melting/boiling behaviour is a test for purity, not just a property to memorise.

activities.title: Chemistry 'pure' vs supermarket 'pure'
feedback: If a learner calls orange juice or spring water 'pure' because it is natural with nothing added, name the two senses explicitly: the advertising sense versus the chemistry sense (one substance only). Spring water is a mixture; distilled water is pure.
If a learner says any clear see-through liquid is pure, point out salt water is clear but a mixture — appearance cannot decide purity; melting/boiling behaviour can.
activities.rationale: Learners commonly import the everyday meaning of 'pure', so an explicit side-by-side contrast of the two senses, supported by particle pictures, addresses a well-documented confusion. This is a reference/clarification scaffold rather than the empirical test itself.
sourceClaims: Students confuse the everyday meaning of 'pure' (natural/unadulterated) with the chemical meaning (single substance)
learnerActions: Examine an everyday label such as '100% pure orange juice — all natural' and decide whether a chemist would call it pure.
Compare a tap-to-reveal contrast of pure-substance and mixture particle pictures alongside annotated sharp-vs-range curves.
Write a sentence distinguishing the two meanings: everyday 'pure' = natural/nothing added; chemical 'pure' = a single element or compound with nothing else in it.
Classify examples: spring water (a mixture), distilled water (pure), salty water (a mixture that still looks clear).
activities.intendedInsight: The scientific meaning of 'pure' differs sharply from everyday use: orange juice and spring water are mixtures even though adverts call them 'pure', because scientifically 'pure' means a single substance only.

activities.title: Formulations: why we deliberately make mixtures
feedback: If a learner assumes 'impure = bad', connect to the examples: a medicine or an alloy is deliberately a mixture because the combination performs better than any single substance alone.

Reinforce that because the components are not chemically joined, each keeps its own chemical identity and the mixture can in principle be separated by physical means — unlike a compound — even though the mixture as a whole may behave differently from its separate components.
activities.rationale: Previewing formulations bridges toward later (KS4) content and corrects an implicit value judgement that pure is always 'better'. This reinforces the mixture-vs-compound distinction at a useful, concrete level.
learnerActions: List everyday designed mixtures — medicines, alloys, paints, fuels — and identify what useful job each component does.
Explain in a sentence why a 'formulation' (a mixture made to a precise composition) is deliberately not pure.

Discuss that the substances in a mixture are not chemically joined, so each keeps its own chemical identity and the mixture can in principle be separated by physical means, even though the mixture as a whole can have useful properties that its separate components lack (for example, an alloy is often harder than the pure metal).
activities.intendedInsight: Not all useful materials are pure: many are formulations — mixtures designed to a precise recipe so each ingredient contributes a needed property. Purity is desirable for identification, but mixtures are often what we actually want.

activities.title: Categorise and read: checking purity from evidence
feedback: If a learner expects a mixture to show one sharp melting point like a pure substance, revisit the heating-curve contrast: a range signals a mixture.
If a learner says water cannot be pure because it contains two elements, clarify that a pure substance is one element OR one compound; water is a single compound, so it is pure.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, curve-matching and graph-reading let learners apply the purity test to new cases and surface residual appearance-based or compound-vs-mixture confusions. This sort can check classification and interpretation but does not itself elicit the learner's own experimental evidence, so it is best used after the hands-on heating comparison.
sourceClaims: A pure substance has a sharp fixed melting/boiling point; a mixture melts/boils over a range — used as a purity test; characteristic properties identify substances (NGSS PS1.A)
learnerActions: Sort given samples as pure substance or mixture, justifying each choice from composition or thermal behaviour rather than appearance.
Match heating curves to 'pure' or 'mixture' labels.
Read a melting point from a graph and state whether the sharp-vs-range shape indicates purity.
Explain whether pure water counts as a pure substance even though it is made of two elements, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Purity can be judged from composition and thermal behaviour — not from how a sample looks — and a compound such as water is still a pure substance because it is one substance throughout.

constraints: The 'formulation' idea (a useful mixture made to a precise composition) is later (KS4/GCSE) content; preview it as a bridge, not a required KS3 assessment outcome.

Particle-picture and meaning-of-'pure' reference panels are clarification scaffolds: they can help learners distinguish the two senses of 'pure' but do not by themselves let a learner run the heating test that defines the purity check, so pair them with the empirical comparison.

Categorisation and graph-reading tasks can check whether learners can apply and interpret the purity test, but they do not elicit the learner's own experimental evidence, so they complement rather than replace the hands-on heating comparison.
Appearance is not a valid purity test: both salt water and distilled water look clear, so activities must base judgements on thermal behaviour or composition.

The 'mixture melts over a range' rule is a standard teaching simplification; present it as the KS3-level signature of a mixture without implying every mixture at every composition has a smeared transition.
If running real heating demos, follow standard safety practice for hot liquids and heat sources appropriate to the age group.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles, not proof that any activity was tested.
Two of the three source claims (NGSS/RSC purity guidance; RSC everyday-vs-chemical 'pure' confusion) were marked verified:false in the original row; treat their evidence strength as unconfirmed.

The original material states salty water boils above 100°C and freezes/melts below 0°C; this is the correct direction of colligative effects (boiling-point elevation, freezing/melting-point depression) and has been preserved. Exact magnitudes depend on salt concentration and are not specified.

Mixtures of fixed composition can in principle show a single eutectic transition; the 'melts over a range' teaching is a deliberate KS3-level simplification and is not presented to learners as a universal law.

The original third error-pattern referenced a prerequisite link for appearance-based purity judgement; the linkage itself is not carried into learner-facing activities, but the underlying misconception is addressed.

The DfE source claim was removed from activity 1 because it supports curriculum-topic coverage rather than the specific heating-curve-as-purity-test principle; it was not reused elsewhere as principle support.

No comparative-efficacy or necessity claims from the original artefact-fit notes (e.g. '3D adds no value', 'an in-role dialogue cannot generate the graph evidence') were propagated as universal laws; they are reframed as narrow scope limits where retained.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: have samples of pure ice and salty-water ice, each with a thermometer as they melt. Ask the child to predict whether both hold at exactly 0°C while melting, and WHY. A child using appearance/everyday-purity predicts both at 0°C. The salty ice melts below 0 and over a range. The pre-observation reasoning about purity is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Salt water and distilled water both look clear. Which is pure, and what single test would prove it?
Why do we deliberately MAKE mixtures like medicines, alloys and paints — what's a 'formulation' for?
If a solid melts over a range 78–85°C instead of sharply at 80°C, what does that tell you?
Is a compound like pure water a 'pure substance' even though it's made of two elements? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: No — to a scientist orange juice is a MIXTURE (water, sugars, acids, pulp…), not pure. 'Pure' scientifically means a SINGLE substance (one element or one compound) with nothing else in it. You test purity by melting/boiling point: a pure substance melts/boils at a single sharp, fixed temperature, while a mixture melts/boils over a RANGE. Full marks need the everyday-vs-scientific distinction PLUS the sharp-melting-point test.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'pure' means natural, clean, or unadulterated (everyday sense) rather than a single substance
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the two meanings explicitly: the advertising sense vs the chemistry sense (one substance only). Spring water is a mixture; distilled water is pure.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — it's pure because it's all natural with nothing added.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: calls orange juice or spring water 'pure' because it's natural/nothing added

errorPatterns.pattern: impurities don't affect melting/boiling points, or a mixture has one melting point like a pure substance
errorPatterns.nextMove: Impurities LOWER and SPREAD the melting point (why salt is put on icy roads). A range signals a mixture; a sharp point signals purity. Show a melting-range comparison.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes, and you could tell because it melts at one exact temperature like pure things do.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: expects a mixture to melt at a single sharp temperature, or can't say what impurities do

errorPatterns.pattern: a mixture must look non-uniform / cloudy, so any clear see-through liquid is pure
errorPatterns.nextMove: Salt water is clear but a mixture; many mixtures look uniform. Appearance can't decide it — the melting/boiling behaviour can.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: judges purity by appearance — clear = pure, cloudy = mixture

responseLevels.gap: Uses the everyday sense of 'pure' (natural/clean); judges purity by appearance; thinks mixtures melt at a single point.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes everyday from scientific purity, uses the sharp-vs-range melting/boiling point as the test, explains impurities lower/spread the melting point, and recognises formulations as deliberately designed mixtures — not judging by appearance.
responseLevels.partial: Gives the scientific definition (single substance) but can't deploy the melting-point-range test, or can't explain why useful formulations are deliberately impure — definition without the diagnostic behaviour.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A carton says '100% pure orange juice — all natural.' In science, would a chemist call orange juice 'pure'? Then the important part: explain what 'pure' means to a scientist, and how you could TEST whether a clear liquid is pure or not.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason separates a child using the scientific definition (single substance; sharp fixed melting point) from one using the everyday sense ('pure' = natural/unadulterated/clean). The melting-point test is the discriminator: only the scientific understanding connects purity to a sharp transition.
